title: Synthesis of Bulk Superconducting LiNbO$_2$ Crystals through CaH$_2$ Reduction
authors: Ryan Paxson, Stephanie J. Hong, Bicky Moirangthem, Parham Kabirifar, Saya Takeuchi, Tianyu Li, Chih-Yu Lee, Haotong Liang, Keenan Avers, Kamal Joshi, Amlan Datta, Makariy Tanatar, Shanta Saha, Peter Zavalij, Ruslan Prozorov, Alexander J. Grutter, Efrain E. Rodriguez, Ichiro Takeuchi
abstract: We have synthesized layered superconducting LiNbO$_2$ crystals through a bulk phase transformation from LiNbO$_3$ single crystals via CaH$_2$ reduction. As the Nb valence is reduced from 5+ to 3+, the material undergoes a structural transformation to the resulting product, LiNbO$_2$, which is accompanied by metallic behavior and a superconducting transition, Tc onset, as high as 14.4 K. Secondary ion mass spectroscopy (SIMS) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) show that the resulting phase is hole-doped through de-lithiation during the reduction. Magnetization and AC susceptibility measurements from a tunnel diode resonator confirm the bulk nature of superconductivity with a superconducting volume fraction of approximately 77% and an upper critical field approaching 26 T. Our study demonstrates extreme hydride reduction as an effective method to induce phase transformations with non-topotactic pathways and can be used to synthesize bulk materials with exotic properties.
summary: This work reports synthesizing bulk superconducting LiNbO2 crystals from LiNbO3 single crystals using CaH2 reduction. The process induces a structural phase change accompanied by metallic behavior and superconductivity up to 14.4 K. Comprehensive characterization confirms the bulk nature of this high-temperature superconductor.
main_problem: The study aims to synthesize bulk superconducting LiNbO2 crystals by inducing a phase transformation from parent LiNbO3 single crystals using CaH2 reduction.
main_result: The reduction successfully yields superconducting LiNbO2 with an onset critical temperature up to 14.4 K and confirms robust, bulk superconductivity via the Meissner effect measurements.
method: Synthesis involves controlled hydride reduction of single crystals, followed by extensive characterization using techniques like XPS, SIMS, AC susceptibility, and magnetization measurements.
model_or_system: The physical system is the solid-state phase transformation from layered LiNbO3 to superconducting LiNbO2. The process involves valence state changes (Nb 5+ to Nb 3+) and stoichiometry modification via de-lithiation and hydrogenation.
key_observables: Superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$ onset $\approx 14.4 	ext{ K}$), superconducting volume fraction ($\approx 77\%$), upper critical field ($H_{c2} \approx 26 	ext{ T}$), and oxidation states derived from XPS ($	ext{Nb}^{3+}$).
important_parameters: Reduction temperature range ($350^\circ	ext{C}$ to $700^\circ	ext{C}$) and reaction time (up to 720 hours); the stoichiometry of the resulting phase.
main_assumptions: The reduction process is modeled as a reconstructive, non-topotactic phase transformation driven by extreme hydride chemistry.
figures_summary: Figures show cross-sectional SEM/EDS mapping confirming bulk conversion; XRD confirms $	ext{LiNbO}_2$ presence; and magnetic measurements confirm the Meissner effect and high $H_{c2}$.
paper_structure: The paper details the synthesis procedure, followed by comprehensive characterization using multiple techniques (SIMS, XPS, Magnetometry) to prove phase transformation, doping mechanisms, and superconducting properties.
why_interesting: While focused on oxides, the study's use of controlled chemical reduction to induce novel electronic states (superconductivity) in a crystalline solid is relevant to understanding emergent quantum phases driven by stoichiometry control, which has parallels in correlated electron systems.
